content: 1. For children aged 2 months to 5 years, assess for danger signs or signs of lower respiratory tract infections (LTI) at a health facility. This involves both the caregiver and the health worker. 2. Conduct a thorough evaluation for infections such as meningitis or pneumonia. This includes asking about symptoms and performing a physical examination using the Look, Listen, Feel approach as per the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines. 3. For neonates, infants, and children, health workers should check for all symptoms by asking relevant questions and conducting physical exams to identify signs of illness. 4. Health promotion and prevention measures should be implemented, including checking the child’s immunization status, vitamin A supplementation, and deworming as appropriate for their age. 5. During Stage 1, register the child and create or update their profile. This includes capturing the reason for the visit and determining whether the child is sick or well. 6. In Stage 2, measure basic anthropometric parameters and assess symptoms and signs. For children under 2 months, focus on specific danger signs. For children aged 2 months to 5 years, assess symptoms such as cough, diarrhea, fever, ear problems, skin or eye issues, anemia, and malnutrition. 7. If life-threatening conditions are suspected, such as sepsis, preterm birth complications, low birth weight, HIV infection, or severe conditions like seizures, jaundice, necrotizing enterocolitis, congenital syphilis, or ophthalmia neonatorum, stabilize the child and refer them for further care. 8. Perform necessary laboratory tests and assessments as indicated by the system. Record all observations and test results in the child’s profile. 9. Classify the child’s condition based on the decision logic provided by the system. Agree or disagree with the classification based on clinical observations. Provide appropriate treatments, advice, and follow-up steps. 10. For well children, ensure health promotion activities are conducted, and follow-up visits are scheduled as needed. If a well child is found to be sick during the visit, reassign them as a sick child and initiate a new consultation. 11. For sick children, provide drug treatments, other necessary interventions, and advice to the caregiver. Document the treatment plan and next steps for follow-up or referral. 12. In emergencies, conduct triage and emergency assessments to identify life-threatening conditions. Stabilize the child and proceed with referral or further management. 13. For newborns, essential newborn care should be provided immediately after birth. This includes determining whether the newborn is healthy or sick and initiating appropriate treatment or referral. 14. Follow-up visits should be conducted to monitor the child’s progress and update their records. Ensure that all past consultations and treatments are reviewed during follow-up. 15. The business process for treating children involves providing caregivers with drug treatments, other interventions, and advice, while also outlining the next steps for follow-up or referral. 16. Health workers should use digital tools and decision-support systems to ensure accurate assessments, classifications, and treatments. These tools help streamline workflows and improve the quality of care provided to children.
